rewrites.summary:
In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body, and the events are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.

Newer reporting profiles the region as a fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, with possible municipal-police participation, and the official answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. A trans visitor therefore stands under a formally protective framework alongside customary exclusion and violent-incident reports at exactly the events tourists attend.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Context that colours the assessment without dominating it: the region's international reputation for diversity accompanies the same reporting that frames it as a fastest-growing tourist paradise, and the official answer of stepped-up visitor security appears within that same reporting frame; the 2024 festival exclusion drew a complaint through the national equality body rather than through any institution of the state itself.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The administrative gender-recognition procedure (12 and above since 2021, fully opened by the 2023 ruling) is a resident route; its openness measures official climate more than it protects a visitor crossing a checkpoint with mismatched documents.

rewrites.summary: Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people, and trans women were 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year across at least 17 states reporting victims - a top-of-table lethality record a visitor must weigh against any formal protections. Its legal gender recognition law (2021) still carries an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, and the state congress has still not corrected the text: for a visitor whose documents must match their presentation, the unmet duty to conform the law to the binding ruling is itself a live hostility signal, and no state-level enforcement data exists to temper it.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Comparisons with neighbours sharpen the record: Mexico City - which also had high counts in 2024-25 - created a transfeminicide investigation unit and a mandatory-response protocol within months; another neighbour, the Estado de Mexico, has had a penal-code hate-crime provision covering bias motives since 2021, though it likewise defies the Supreme Court ruling on recognition. This state itself has neither the court-compliant text nor any criminal-law protection or enforcement innovation - a contrast with its peers rather than a visitor-facing rule in itself.
rewrites.localsOnly:
For residents, the recognition law is a document route left in non-compliance: the 2021 state civil-code reform keeps the 18-year minimum-age requirement the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, and the congress has not corrected the text.

There is no dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, and no state-level enforcement data, so the recorded 2025 homicides describe residents without any state mechanism backed by published numbers.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No state-level enforcement data exists, so the on-the-ground operation of the non-compliant recognition text is unresolved. Whether the congress will conform the law to the court ruling is not reported. This record contains no border-screening information for visitors; its document-procedure content is limited to the recognition-law points above.

rewrites.summary:
This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 people crossing the long, porous international border - including seven transgender people - in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to the financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power. On the audited record there is no statute criminalising trans presence here; the documented harm is police practice at the checkpoints.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context: the checkpoint operations run within a wider national border-enforcement framework applied along the long, porous international frontier, and the detained travellers were en route to the financial capital, marking the smuggling corridor inside which the gender-appearance-as-disguise profiling occurs. The national welfare-board rules under which the state's board was constituted are a parent-country framework whose real functioning the record cannot measure beyond the right-to-information findings.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: welfare-board machinery and fake-identity-document crackdowns on local residents; the checkpoint sweeps are the visitor-relevant element. This state is one of only twelve to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but the right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: General border-security enforcement along the Bangladesh frontier (people smuggling, document fraud) affects all travellers and residents of border districts; only the gender-appearance-as-disguise framing is trans-relevant. Whether the state's own welfare board is among the inactive majority found by the right-to-information investigation is not specified.

rewrites.summary:
West Bengal replicates the checkpoint script documented in its neighbour: police arrested a transgender person arriving from across the long, porous international border for allegedly "infiltrating", treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity. It is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating that some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime occurs at a detectable rate.

The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than a repeated-sweep pattern elsewhere: the documented record here is a single arrest plus the broader infiltration framing. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism - trans presentation treated as evidence of illegal entry.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The comparative layer colours the assessment rather than driving it: on the national comparative index this state sits slightly below the national average, its neighbour shows a repeated-operations pattern, and a large peer - sharing the profiling language - has a strong offsetting civic infrastructure this state lacks. The same border-policing logic governs the frontier these records share.
rewrites.localsOnly: The Transgender Persons Act cases recorded in this state and the state welfare board's nominal operations concern residents' access to protection machinery; the checkpoint arrest pattern is what reaches trans-presenting visitors crossing the land border. The recorded 2021 cases (3 of 7 nationally) and the right-to-information finding - that the constituted welfare board operates without a functioning policy framework - are resident-facing data; police also detained the local e-rickshaw driver who carried the arrested person from the border, part of the enforcement reach over residents who assist crossings.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: General cross-border crime and immigration enforcement in the border belt affects all populations; only the trans-appearance-as-infiltration-evidence framing is state-policy relevant to trans travellers. The underlying news report was not retrievable at fetch time (access-denied block), so the arrest account rests on the source summary awaiting re-verification.

rewrites.summary:
In Amritsar - the spiritual centre of the region's dominant faith - the annual Pride assembly cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade after "mounting resistance" from the faith's religious organisations, including a prominent faction and the faith's highest temporal authority; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason. No other law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears in the audited sources for this record.

For a trans visitor the documented signal is institutional, not criminal: no statute here targets trans people, but an organised religious authority compelled the cancellation of the region's annual public trans assembly, and the event simply did not happen. Public trans visibility therefore carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition, and the absence of any recorded state intervention to preserve the event is part of that record.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent institutional context: the opposition came from the faith's religious organisations - a prominent faction and the faith's highest temporal authority - and no recorded state intervention preserved the event. The national framework stands in the background: the same national act under which trans visitors stand decriminalised same-sex conduct and recognised self-identified gender, so a parent-nation framework rather than any regional statute governs a visitor's legal standing here.
rewrites.localsOnly: The record carries no resident-specific discrimination data: the resident-facing element is the cancellation itself - organisers withdrew the region's annual public trans assembly in the face of the faith's highest temporal authority's opposition, and the event did not take place. No status change or resident policy effect is documented beyond that cancellation.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The underlying news report behind the cancellation account carries an unverified fetch history: the record URL is malformed and the page was never cached, returning 404, so that account rests on the source summary. That no other law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears here is a statement about these audited sources, not a claim that none exists.

The national-framework page: in 2018 the country's highest court struck down the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, holding that sexual-orientation discrimination violates the constitution; in 2024 the penal code was replaced by a new code omitting that criminalisation provision. A 2014 ruling recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, codified by the national trans-protection act of 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. The page carries no state/province-specific law or institution targeting trans people.

The national trans-protection act page: the 2019 act grants the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without surgery, bans discrimination, creates a national council for trans people, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus fines for crimes against trans people, with criticism that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education; in January 2020 the highest court issued notice in a petition challenging the act's constitutionality. This is the protective national statute a trans visitor stands under.

rewrites.summary: Tamil Nadu is the country's most protective sub-national regime for trans visitors. It was the first state to introduce a transgender welfare policy (1995), maintains a dedicated Transgender Welfare Board, and adopted a comprehensive State Policy for Transgender Persons in 2025. On 4 August 2025 the Madras High Court expressly commended the policy as "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle" - active judicial confirmation of executive protection that is rare and meaningful for a visitor's institutional recourse. The state was also the only one recording a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020 (1 of 1 nationally) and logged 7 of the 11 national cases in 2023 - its courts are demonstrably being used.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Comparative context: on the national comparative index this state sits above a neighbouring state - this state adds the explicit court commendation and a longer institutional history - and above another, where a religious authority vetoed a trans public assembly, exactly the contrast with the actively protective machinery of this state. No litigation flux or parent-nation turbulence is documented in the audited record.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The board's resident-facing machinery - membership ID cards, free surgery, housing, scholarships, state employment quotas - benefits trans residents; what a visitor encounters is the institutional climate these signal. The dedicated board has operated under a designated administrative title since 15 April 2008, the welfare policy has been in place since 1995, and the local administrative categories are embedded in governance - resident-facing architecture.

A complicating local signal: local transgender devotees in the temple city announced a fast in December 2025 over temple lamp-lighting decisions - trans people acting as political participants in local governance, not evidence of state suppression.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The high-court order behind the 2025 commendation was not retrievable at fetch time (never cached), so the commendation rests on the source summary rather than a fresh re-read of the judgment. The "most protective" framing is relative to the national comparative index, not an absolute standard beyond audited sources.

rewrites.summary:
The state holds a constituted Transgender Welfare Board - one of the 12 states/UTs reported to the federal parliament in December 2021 as having set one up under the national trans-protection rules - and its law-enforcement machinery is measurably engaged: the state registered 2 of the 7 national cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 4 of the 11 recorded in 2023, among the highest sub-national totals in those years.

That activity should be read with the source's own caveat: national recording is sparse (20 cases across 2019-23) because of police registration bias, against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence. Registered cases therefore evidence a system that at least accepts complaints, not rarity of violence. No state-specific restriction is documented; for a trans visitor the picture is one of institutional recognition machinery in a state where such machinery exists and is used.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context: the welfare-board constitution list runs through a national government reply to the national parliament in December 2021, a parent-nation channel rather than a regional rule; this state's case counts are among the highest sub-national totals in the audited national series, and no litigation flux or policy turbulence is documented beyond that series and the caveat above.
rewrites.localsOnly: The overseas scholarship scheme and board benefit measures are resident-facing programmes; their visitor-facing content is the signal of state commitment.
